findings.title: The write step's re-read is not inside a transaction unless it starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE
findings.why_it_matters: D2's safety argument is that the fresh re-read and the watermark stamp are atomic with the vector writes, but the design never says how the transaction opens. Both ways of building it from the text as written fail. Under Python's default mode the re-read runs in autocommit, another writer can commit before the first DML, and the stamp is decided from stale data, which is the false watermark the design exists to prevent. With an explicit deferred `BEGIN`, a commit landing after the re-read makes the first write fail instantly with `database is locked`, because `busy_timeout` doesn't apply to that upgrade, and that loss lands right after the expensive inference.
findings.chosen: Add to D2's pinned list: "The write step runs `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` before the re-read, then re-reads, checks, writes, prunes, stamps, and commits, so `busy_timeout` waits for the lock and nothing can commit between the check and the stamp. A test interleaves a competing commit between the read and the first write." This doesn't need extending to D3's clear or D4's sentinel as operational-resilience proposed: each is a single-statement write with no earlier read to upgrade from, and the probe shows that form succeeds and takes the normal busy wait. If Finding 6 makes the sentinel conditional on a re-read, it needs `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` too.

findings.title: A branch that stays eligible is re-selected at the head of every later batch, then aborts the run
findings.why_it_matters: The Posture and D4 say a lost write "costs one item" and "the run continues", but neither says how the failed branch is left out. Selection is `ORDER BY id LIMIT 20` with no exclusion, so with per-branch commits the unfinished branch is the lowest eligible id and sits first in every later batch. It gets inferred again each time, which is a retry loop despite the "no retries" stance. When it's the only branch left, the batch repeats, `run_batch_loop` calls `on_stuck`, and the run ends with `EXIT_ABORT`. The 20-branch batch no longer maps to a commit boundary, but the stuck guard still assumes it does.
findings.recommended: A: Forward-only pass: `select_batch_cb` adds `AND id > ?` using the last id seen, so a run never revisits a branch
findings.chosen: A: Forward-only pass: `select_batch_cb` adds `AND id > ?` using the last id seen, so a run never revisits a branch

findings.title: "Current chunk" is undefined, and the existing predicate can't prove a vector exists
findings.why_it_matters: D2 says a vector doesn't replace a chunk "already current at equal or better quality", and stamps by `_should_stamp_watermark`'s conditions, but that predicate checks only version, hash, and cap, not model or `chunk_vec` presence. D5 removes the pre-delete that today handles version-stale, wrong-model, and vector-less chunks, so D2's skip rule now has to recognize them. Read as "hash and cap match", the skip would refuse the replacement D5 selected: the branch stays eligible and re-infers without ever healing, which then feeds Finding 2. The next `EMBEDDING_VERSION` bump is the case that hits this, because every chunk is then version-stale with a matching hash.
findings.chosen: Add to D2: "A chunk is current when its `content_hash` matches, its `embedding_version` and `embedding_model` are current, and a `chunk_vec` row exists. D2's write-skip additionally requires `effective_cap_tokens` at least that of the vector being written; the stamp requires `MODEL_TOKEN_LIMIT`. Backfill's diff (D5) selects the same chunks this excludes. Sync's diff stays narrower per H6." Update D2's lock-time row from about 4 ms to about 10 ms to include the vector-presence check.

findings.title: Skip, discard, and withheld-stamp outcomes have no specified log line
findings.why_it_matters: The design adds outcomes that run unattended and leave a branch unembedded: sync skipping inference for a live backfill (D7), a vector discarded on hash mismatch (D2), and a stamp withheld because the proof failed. The Posture only requires logging a failed embed and a write timeout. Without lines for the rest, you can't tell whether Finding 2 is happening, how often D7 delays vectors, or why a branch remains unembedded. These are dark operations under `logging.md`, which requires a signal from unattended processes.
findings.chosen: Add to the Posture's Failure handling line: "Each outcome that leaves a branch unembedded logs a line with the branch id: sync's backfill skip at INFO with the marker PID, and the write step's discarded-on-hash count and withheld stamp at INFO. The backfill's existing completion line adds the count of branches attempted and not updated." This is log lines only, and the "no new metrics" stance stands.

findings.title: D7 infers backfill liveness from a PID marker, so a reused PID silences sync inference
findings.why_it_matters: D7 decides "a backfill is inferring" from `os.kill(pid, 0)` on a marker, which proves only that some process has that PID. A SIGKILLed or OOM-killed backfill leaves its marker behind because the CLI's `finally` never runs. If that PID is later reused, sync skips inference for as long as the other process lives, and the same marker already blocks the next backfill, so new sessions get no vectors. Keyword search and stored messages are unaffected, and vectors catch up once the marker clears.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stale backfill marker whose PID gets reused makes sync skip inference until that process exits or the marker is removed
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stale backfill marker whose PID gets reused makes sync skip inference until that process exits or the marker is removed

findings.title: The content-error sentinel is decided from a snapshot that may be stale
findings.why_it_matters: D4 writes the `-1` sentinel after `_model_still_healthy`. With inference outside any transaction, the content that failed may have changed by then, so the sentinel lands on a branch whose current content was never tried. Selection excludes `-1`, and a tool-content repair doesn't reset it, so the branch stays out of backfill until a later sync clears it or a link change does.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch whose content changes during a failing inference can carry the sentinel until a later sync or link change resets it
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch whose content changes during a failing inference can carry the sentinel until a later sync or link change resets it

findings.title: Backfill has no check for a sync already inferring, so peaks can briefly stack
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: 15 GB machines running manual backfill during active use. D7 checks only at the start of sync's inference, so a backfill starting during a sync's inference can overlap it, up to about 12.4 GB of inference at worst. The critic's "kills the box" is stronger than the arithmetic: 12.4 GB fits in 15 GB unless other load is high, and it needs both processes on near-cap text at once. D7's ratification already accepts this overlap by name.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a backfill starting during a sync's inference can briefly stack both memory peaks
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a backfill starting during a sync's inference can briefly stack both memory peaks

findings.title: An inference that exceeds memory kills the run with nothing naming the branch
findings.why_it_matters: An OOM kill bypasses the sentinel path, which only handles Python exceptions, and leaves no record of which branch was running. Since selection is by id, a repeat kill would stop each run at the same point. The change itself improves this, because every earlier branch is now committed, and the critic asks for no design change.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an OOM kill during backfill doesn't record which branch was running
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an OOM kill during backfill doesn't record which branch was running
